newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat pushes for Hebron deal by year's end.
newsitem.headline: Arafat pushes for Hebron deal by year's end.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has told his peace negotiators to press ahead to clinch a deal this year on a long-overdue Israeli troop pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"The instructions of the president to us were to finish the agreement before the end of the year," chief negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters after a Palestinian cabinet meeting ended early on Saturday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Palestinian security officials earlier to hammer out details of security arrangements for Hebron after 80 percent of the town comes under Palestinian self-rule.
Jibril Rajoub, Palestinian preventive security chief for the West Bank, said the session paved the way for top-level meetings between Arafat, Netanyahu and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.
"I believe we are very close to completing the agreement," Rajoub told reporters. "The subjects of contention are limited."
He said Arafat would meet Mordechai on Sunday and hold talks with Netanyahu later but he did not specify exactly when.
Netanyahu has sought to bolster safeguards for the 400 Jewish settlers who live and study in heavily-armed compounds in the heart of Hebron, a town of 100,000 Palestinians.

Netanyahu's office said he spoke to Arafat at the behest of the Palestinian negotiating team. "The prime minister said... that he is standing firm concerning the security requirements of Israel in Hebron," it said in a statement.

The Hebron talks, which only recently appeared near collapse, were energised by a peace shuttle by U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross. Ross, who nudged Netanyahu and Arafat into meeting on Tuesday, was due back in the Middle East on Monday.
Erekat said he met Netanyahu's policy adviser, Dore Gold, on Friday to discuss the continued implementation of interim Israeli-Palestinian peace deals after a Hebron accord was struck.

He said the sides were stuck over a Palestinian demand that Israel must commit itself to a detailed timetable for further troop withdrawals from rural West Bank lands as specified by a 1995 accord signed by Israel's previous left-leaning government.
"There are different opinions but we hope that we can overcome these issues in the next few days," Erekat said.

Hebron remained tense after four petrol bombs were thrown at Israeli army posts near Jewish settler enclaves in the heart of the town, which is holy to Moslems and Jews and a bastion of militancy for both.
In a move to ease the atmosphere, the Israeli army said it would re-open Hebron University, closed 10 months ago after a wave of Islamist suicide bombings killed scores of people in Israel.
"The opening of the university was possible after the institute's management committed to keep law and order there," an army spokesman said.
Hebron is the last of seven major West Bank towns occupied in the 1967 Middle East war that Israel agreed to turn over to the Palestinian Authority under the 1995 self-rule deal.
